beats.trigger: ## Evaluations
beats.got: nothing new, a title

beats.trigger: The generator sharpens against that feedback while you walk away.
beats.got: Something runs a loop and improves a thing while I'm out of the room. I'm not sure what thing yet.

beats.trigger: Start with the judge you saved at the close of Module 5.
beats.got: Reading homework, and I didn't do Module 5 properly.

beats.trigger: **Build** a self-improving eval loop: separate agents generate and judge, the Module 5 judge scores each round unchanged
beats.got: Learning-objective list. One agent writes, another marks it, and the marker doesn't change.

beats.trigger: Can agents improve if you define the outcome and let them find the path, or does organisational mess still matter too much?
beats.got: The question is fair. Organisational mess is the thing that killed the last three programmes, so someone is at least asking it.

beats.trigger: the system absorbs the catches without you.
beats.got: Marketing line. 'Without you' is exactly what makes my people nervous.

beats.trigger: Humans will not cope with all the detail for long. You can stay inside one loop. You cannot stay inside all of them.
beats.got: Nobody can read everything, so you write down what good means and let a checker apply it. That is just quality control.

beats.trigger: You saved the winner as `judges/groundedness-judge.md`: measured judgment, made runnable.
beats.got: A reusable checklist saved as a file. Fine, I'd call that a test script.

beats.trigger: every name appears in the source, every number traces to a file, every claim cites evidence or admits the gap.
beats.got: A check that the machine isn't making things up. That is a real worry and a concrete one.

beats.trigger: Two mails both avoid overclaiming; one is forgettable, the other makes the reader act.
beats.got: Correct isn't enough. You also need a check for 'is it useful', which is the harder one to write.

beats.trigger: If the judge moved, the score means nothing.
beats.got: Fix the marker, change only the writer, and compare. That is basic method and I can check the file hash myself.

beats.trigger: The answer is never "the eval passed."
beats.got: A passed test proves little unless the test checks the right thing.

beats.trigger: Example run note: *round 1 flagged 11 claims, round 2 flagged 6, round 3 flagged 3.*
beats.got: Three rounds, and a number that goes down. At least there is a number.

beats.trigger: Note what the judge catches; the tactic must learn that.
beats.got: I run it once by hand and see what it flags. Doing it myself beats being told.

beats.trigger: Now step away. Come back to a tactic tightened by a judge you did not move.
beats.got: I start it, go for coffee, and it has rewritten its own instructions when I'm back. That wasn't possible two years ago, or not like this.

beats.trigger: The score means something only if the judge stayed still: the SHA in `module-6/eval-notes.md` must match.
beats.got: I can verify the claim with a checksum instead of believing the agent. That is what I wanted.

beats.trigger: And you weren't there.
beats.got: Nothing new. Said before in different words.

beats.trigger: PDCA at the eval layer: Plan (generation tactic), Do (generate), Check (judge), Act (rewrite tactic).
beats.got: PDCA. We had that in 2012. Same cycle, new actors.

beats.trigger: Convergence was the floor in Module 5. Eval-as-yardstick is the ceiling here.
beats.got: Floor and ceiling again. I can reuse the loop around a different judge.

beats.trigger: That does not mean the work is done.
beats.got: Zero flags doesn't mean it's good. Agreed.

beats.trigger: A flat score is information about the judge, not the work.
beats.got: A green dashboard says the thing being measured is fine, not that the work is. Every programme steering group needs to hear that.

beats.trigger: A generator that grades itself passes itself.
beats.got: Score a handful by hand and compare with the judge before trusting it. It admits the checker has never been checked, and I can do that in an afternoon.

beats.trigger: No release so far has told anyone what good means in your company.
beats.got: The tool gets better but 'what good looks like here' stays our job. Plausible, and modest.

beats.trigger: The destination is not "the human disappears." You move one level up: you design the loop and own the yardstick.
beats.got: A recap of earlier modules, plus 'you become the designer'. That is the line every transformation uses for what happens to people.

beats.trigger: What would have to be true before you let the agent hit send?
beats.got: A practical question: what conditions would make me trust it to send. A usable checklist.

beats.trigger: An ungrounded mail is a trust problem. A grounded but vague or tone-deaf mail is a usefulness problem.
beats.got: Same floor and ceiling point a third time.

beats.trigger: Variety in, selection out, memory keeps
beats.got: A slogan for generate, pick, save. Nothing new.

beats.trigger: Some categories never go without a human.
beats.got: Autonomy comes in steps, from draft only up to send automatically, and some things always keep a person. That is candid and it is how I'd run it.

beats.trigger: Two judges now sit on disk: one keeps the work grounded, one steers it toward your standard.
beats.got: I write down my standard for an internal mail as a second check. Concrete enough.

beats.trigger: Every clean week is evidence the loop works, and each one erodes your ability to tell when the loop stops.
beats.got: The better the system performs, the worse I get at noticing when it fails. It says that against its own pitch.

beats.trigger: This check has no instrument, only a date: when did you last read one of these start to finish, without the agent summarising it first?
beats.got: Put a date in the calendar and read one real output myself. Cheap, and I'll do it.

beats.trigger: Your role in the loop is to design the conditions under which the system earns more autonomy, one loop at a time.
beats.got: Closing-slide wording. Sounds like the last programme's target-state picture.

beats.trigger: The judge file stays untouched: that's the integrity of the loop.
beats.got: Ask the agent to sharpen its rules further and keep the judge file as is. Fine.

beats.trigger: Which rule did you claim to remove but keep under another name? Quote both lines.
beats.got: A way to test the agent's summary against its own files instead of trusting its tone. I'd use that.

beats.trigger: A flat score is information about the judge, not the work.
beats.got: Four-line summary. The flat-score line is the one I keep.

beats.trigger: Pick one call that should run through the eval loop before anyone relies on it, and write the trigger into your working notes.
beats.got: Homework: pick one real task to put through the loop. It could work if the task is small.

beats.trigger: Trust the loop you can inspect.
beats.got: Trust only what you can inspect. I can accept that.

take_homes: A green score only tells you the checker is satisfied. Check the checker by hand on a handful of outputs, and keep the writer and the checker separate.
Fix the judge and change only the writer, then verify with a file hash. I can test that myself without taking anyone's word.
The more it works, the less I look. So read one real output myself on a date in the calendar.

monday.move: Take one recurring internal summary my team produces, try the judge and loop on it once, and read the output start to finish myself.
monday.who: Me, with one analyst from my team
monday.when: One afternoon next week, only if the programme steering group doesn't take it
monday.stop_condition: If the judge passes things I would send back, I drop it. If it flags real misses, I try a second report.
monday.blocker: My calendar, the leftover programme steering groups, and that I skipped part of Module 5.

misconception.why: The checksum check and the admission that nothing scores the judge were things I could test myself, which the earlier programmes never gave me. The loop itself is still PDCA with new actors, and the autonomy wording sounds like the last deck. I still think wait-and-see is safer, but I would run one small test first.

one_line: Mostly the quality-control cycle again, but it was honest that nobody checks the checker and that you stop looking once it works, and I can test the loop myself.
